Two of the eight highlight a name and so open with Who, which needs no inversion at all; those are the ones to start a hesitant child on.

G2-357.h1: Ask About the Picture: Why and How
G2-357.title: Ask Why and How Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-357.metaDescription: Question words worksheet: four picture tiles and six ruled lines, each already begun with Who, What, Where, When, Why or How. Finish each question.
G2-357.p1: Four picture tiles run across the top of this 2nd grade page — on the sheet shown a person, a pear, a house and a clock face set to nine o'clock. Beneath them sit six wide sets of handwriting rules, and each one already carries its first word in grey: Who, What, Where, When, Why and How. The child finishes every line so that it becomes a question about the pictures. Nothing else is printed, and no answer is expected anywhere on the sheet.
G2-357.p2: The title names the two starters that are new here. Who, what, where and when have all appeared on earlier faces of the family; why and how have not, because neither can be answered by pointing at a thing, and both need the child to invent a situation rather than read one. That is the open end of the question-word ladder and the reason this page has no right answers — a good why is the one nobody else at the table thought of.
G2-357.p3: One sheet, six questions. The four tiles are separate pictures rather than one scene, so decide as a class what is happening between them before anyone writes; the why and how lines have very little to work with otherwise. Use it to close a question-words unit, and read the six finished questions aloud — they are usually better than the pictures deserve.

G2-346.title: Rounding to the Nearest 10 Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free PDF
G2-346.metaDescription: Rounding worksheet: fourteen numbers each followed by a box, with a worked example of 47 and a digit strip splitting 0 to 4 from 5 to 9 at the top.
G2-346.p1: Fourteen numbers are set out in two columns on this 2nd grade page, each followed by an approximately-equal sign and one dashed box. A reference band across the top does two things at once: it works 47 into 50 with the ones digit picked out in coral, and it prints the digits 0 to 9 in two groups with a down arrow over the first five and an up arrow over the rest. The sheet shown runs 76, 79, 45, 633, 268, 267, 85, 53, 522, 54, 549, 67, 658 and 111.
G2-346.p2: Everything the page asks for is decided by one digit, and the strip is there so a child can check which half it falls in without being told again. Two of the fourteen end in five, the case where the rule has to be a rule rather than a judgement of which ten is nearer, and half the numbers are three digits long, so the tens place has to be found before it can be rounded rather than simply read off the front.
G2-346.p3: One sheet, fourteen numbers, fourteen boxes. This is the base page of the rounding family and the one with the most practice on it; the five faces built on it change the place, the direction or the shape of the task rather than adding more of the same. Keep the reference band visible, since every sibling page reprints it with a different worked example.

G3-387.h1: Rounding Up or Down? Sort the Numbers
G3-387.title: Rounding Up or Down Worksheet for 3rd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G3-387.metaDescription: Rounding worksheet: twelve numbers in circles and two bins headed round down and round up. Write each number into the bin its ones digit sends it to.
G3-387.p1: Twelve numeral chips sit in a panel on this 3rd grade page — 481, 52, 329, 418, 85, 65, 549, 647, 426, 24, 72 and 13 on the sheet shown — and two large bins stand below, one headed round down with a falling arrow and one headed round up with a rising one. Each bin is divided into nine empty cells. The child decides which way each number goes to the nearest ten and writes it into a cell in the right bin.
G3-387.p2: The rounded answer is never written on this page, which is the whole idea: the task is the decision and nothing else, so a child who can round but cannot say why gets no cover from the arithmetic. Six of the chips are two digits and six are three, and two of them end in five, so the rule has to be applied rather than felt. Seven go up and five go down, an uneven split that stops the bins being filled alternately.
G3-387.p3: One sheet, twelve chips, two bins. Each bin is printed with nine cells, more than either will need, so several will be left empty and that is expected rather than a sign of a missed number. This is the decision face of the rounding family; use it between the nearest-ten base page and the nearest-hundred sheet, where the same decision moves one place to the left.

G3-388.title: Rounding to the Nearest 100 Worksheet for 3rd Grade | Free PDF
G3-388.metaDescription: Rounding worksheet: fourteen three-digit numbers each with one box, rounded to the nearest hundred by reading the tens digit. Worked example 472 to 500.
G3-388.p1: Fourteen three-digit numbers fill this 3rd grade page in two columns, each with a single dashed box beside it. The reference band at the top works 472 into 500 with the tens digit marked in coral, and reprints the digit strip with 0 to 4 under a falling arrow and 5 to 9 under a rising one. The sheet shown runs 462, 350, 572, 467, 236, 397, 489, 328, 317, 874, 540, 851, 848 and 532. Every answer is a whole hundred.
G3-388.p2: One place to the left is the only change from the base page, and it is the change children get wrong, because the digit that decides is no longer the last one. That is why the instruction names the tens digit outright and why the worked example marks the 7 of 472 rather than the 2. Two of the fourteen sit exactly halfway — 350 and 540 — and 397 is the one that rounds up across a hundred boundary, from three hundred and something to 400.
G3-388.p3: One sheet, fourteen numbers, fourteen boxes. It is deliberately the same shape as the nearest-ten base page so the two can be set side by side and compared; the numbers are all between 101 and 949, so no answer is 0 or 1000. Print the round-to-both face afterwards, which asks for the ten and the hundred of one number at the same time.

G3-389.title: Round and Estimate the Sum Worksheet for 3rd Grade | Free PDF
G3-389.metaDescription: Estimation worksheet: eight two-digit additions, each with a box for the first rounded number, a box for the second, and a box for their total.
G3-389.p1: Eight additions are printed one to a row on this 3rd grade page, each followed by three dashed boxes: one for the first number rounded, one for the second, and one for the two rounded numbers added. The reference band works 23 plus 48 into 20 plus 50 equals 70. The sheet shown runs 12 plus 51, 29 plus 14, 59 plus 19, 31 plus 32, 35 plus 28, 15 plus 36, 38 plus 52 and 63 plus 27, so every estimate stays at or under one hundred.
G3-389.p2: This is the only face in the family that puts rounding to work, and the three boxes keep the two steps apart so a child cannot add first and round afterwards. Both numbers have to be handled before the addition can start, which is twice the decision of the base page for the same number of rows. Two of the eight estimates happen to land on the exact sum, which is a useful thing to notice and a good question to ask at the end.
G3-389.p3: One sheet, eight additions, twenty-four boxes. The addends are all two digits and the totals stay inside a hundred, so the final column can be done in the head once the rounding is on the page. Give it after the base and the sort faces, when rounding is quick enough that it does not swamp the estimating it is supposed to serve.

G3-390.title: Which Numbers Round to 50 Worksheet for 3rd Grade | Free PDF
G3-390.metaDescription: Rounding worksheet: a target of 50 above a staggered field of sixteen numbers from 31 to 64. Circle every one that rounds to the ten at the top.
G3-390.p1: Sixteen numbers sit in a loose staggered field on this 3rd grade page, with a single coral target pill above them reading approximately 50. The numbers on the sheet shown are 31, 46, 36, 55, 49, 44, 63, 51, 47, 45, 35, 58, 52, 64, 57 and 32. The child circles every one that rounds to fifty and leaves the rest. Six of the sixteen qualify. The reference band at the top works a different example, 83 into 80, so the target is not given away twice.
G3-390.p2: Running the rule backwards is what this face is for. Instead of one number with one answer, the child is given the answer and asked which numbers could have produced it, which is the question that reveals whether rounding is understood as a range or only as a procedure. Both edges of that range are on the page: 45 is in and 44 is out, 54 would be in and 55 is out, so the halfway rule decides two of the sixteen on its own.
G3-390.p3: One sheet, sixteen numbers, six to circle. Ask afterwards for the smallest and the largest number that would have worked — 45 and 54 — because naming the two ends is the understanding this page is testing. It is the only inverse face in the rounding family and the one to use when the forward pages have become easy.

G3-391.title: Rounding to 10 and 100 Worksheet for 3rd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G3-391.metaDescription: Rounding worksheet: eight three-digit numbers with two boxes each, one headed nearest ten and one nearest hundred, so one number gets two answers.
G3-391.p1: Eight three-digit numbers run down this 3rd grade page, each with two dashed boxes beside it under a pair of headings: nearest ten and nearest hundred. The sheet shown asks for 159, 494, 791, 305, 353, 535, 567 and 556. The reference band works the same number, 472, twice over — once to 470 with the ones digit marked and once to 500 with the tens digit marked — so the two answers of one number are shown side by side before any are asked for.
G3-391.p2: Every other rounding face names one place and keeps it. This one puts both on the same line, which is the only way to show that rounding has no single answer until the place is fixed: 494 is 490 and it is also 500, and neither is wrong. The digit that decides moves for each box, so a child must relocate it eight times over rather than settle into one habit — the ones digit for the first box, the tens digit for the second.
G3-391.p3: One sheet, eight numbers, sixteen boxes. Go back to the original number for the second box rather than rounding the first answer again; on this sheet the two routes agree, but they do not always, and the habit is worth forming here. Print it last in the rounding family, after the separate nearest-ten and nearest-hundred pages it puts together.

findings: K-360 — HARD DEFECT. The card reading 'How many fingers?' is illustrated with body parts/finger@3x, a closed fist with ONE index finger raised. The configured answer is 10 (b4var-rows/human-body.js mix {1:2, 2:3, 10:1}). The picture argues for 1 as strongly as a picture can. Either the answer or the art is wrong; hand@3x (five splayed digits) is the cheaper fix.

G1-356 — HARD DEFECT. Three of the six numbered markers are printed ON TOP of the very feature they name. Marker 1 (mouth, 5 letter boxes) covers the smile: only the two corner tips show outside the coral disc. Marker 5 (knee) covers the right leg's knee crease, and the only crease still visible on the page is the LEFT leg's. Marker 6 (toe) covers two toes. The instruction says 'Find each numbered part on the figure'; only the letter-box count rescues the task. Parts confirmed from data-lcs-parts='mouth,arm,elbow,hand,knee,toe'.

G2-357 — HARD DEFECT. The Why line has no referent. The instruction reads 'Look at the picture' (singular) but the page prints four unrelated tiles: a construction worker, a pear, a house and a clock at 9:00. There is no scene, no event and no relation between them, so there is nothing a 'Why ...?' question can be about. The design calls it 'one four-tile scene'; the render is four separate tiles side by side.

G2-357 — the title names 'Why and How' while the page prints SIX starters (data-lcs-kinds='who,what,where,when,why,how'). The design intends the title to name only the two NEW starters; a teacher reading the title expects two ruled lines and finds six.

G3-391 — the notation invites a wrong method and the shipped pool hides it. Each row reads '159 [approx] [box] [approx] [box]', so the second approximation sign takes the FIRST BOX as its visible left operand, i.e. round to the ten and then round that answer to the hundred, which is not the same operation. All eight shipped numbers (159, 494, 791, 305, 353, 535, 567, 556) give the same result either way, so a child who adopts the chain is never corrected. The counterexample class is trivially reachable: tens digit 4 with ones 5 or more, e.g. 449 to 450 to 500, but 449 to 400. Either repeat the base number before the second sign, or seed one such number into the pool.

G3-386 — the rule table prints even+even, odd+odd and even+odd but NOT odd+even. Three of the twelve cards present the odd addend first (549+858, 861+316, 129+720), so a child following the instruction to 'use the table' cannot find their combination and must already know that order does not matter, which is precisely what the page has not taught.

G1-364 — the word bank holds FIVE materials for EIGHT rows (metal x2, paper x2, cardboard x2, plastic x1, glass x1) and the instruction 'Write the word from the bank on the line' never says a word may be reused. The base page G1-350 and the sibling K-354 both use closed one-to-one banks, so the convention a child brings to this page is the wrong one. Same class: G1-374 (five bank words, six rows, 'What' twice) and G1-371 (three words, eight rows).

G1-351 / G3-387 / G1-372 / G1-375 — the answer grid is sized to a maximum rather than to the draw, on four faces across three families. G1-351 prints eight boxes per house for a 5-odd / 4-even split of nine numbers: 7 of 16 boxes have nothing to receive. G3-387 prints nine cells per bin for a 7-up / 5-down split of twelve chips: 6 of 18 cells stay empty. G1-372 prints three columns of six ruled lines for a 5/3/2 split of ten names: 7 lines unused. G1-375 prints three bins of seven lines for three tiles each: 12 lines unused. Nothing on any of the four sheets tells a child the grid will not fill.

K-364 — the symbol legend occupies the eighth cell of a 4x2 grid whose other seven cells are labelled days (Monday to Sunday) and it carries NO heading of its own. A child, and a teacher scanning the sheet, reads it as an eighth day.

K-365 — the instruction says 'use the key to see if it is cold, warm or hot' but the words cold, warm and hot appear NOWHERE on the page. The key prints three thermometers against three garments and nothing else; the scales carry tick marks and tinted bands but no numerals (deliberate for K), so the mapping from a band height to one of the three named words is never made on paper.

K-365 — hot is signalled by SUNGLASSES and warm by a T-shirt. A T-shirt is worn when it is warm AND when it is hot; sunglasses signal sun, not heat. The warm/hot boundary rests on an arbitrary garment pairing rather than on anything the picture shows.
